findings.problem: Every resource limit (blob size, ops, parents, message, DAG depth, publication size, tree entries) is a compile-time default and there is no way for an operator to override them in a real deployment. `Limits` has no serde/env/config constructor, `RepoConfig` (.ag/config.json, crates/ag-integrate/src/layout.rs:72) has no limits section, and the only production construction is `let limits = Limits::default();` in crates/ag-integrate/src/repo.rs:140. The values are only overridable by editing struct fields in tests. The server also re-hardcodes two of them when advertising limits (crates/ag-server/src/api/session.rs:44-45: `max_changeset_ops: 100_000`, `max_changesets_per_publication: 10_000`), so if limits were ever tuned the negotiated values would be wrong for clients. Related hardcode in ag-integrate/src/history.rs:184 (`.min(5_000_000)`).
findings.proposed_fix: Derive Serialize/Deserialize (with `#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]`) on `Limits`, add an optional `limits` section to `RepoConfig` (additive, format stays 1) plus env/CLI overrides (e.g. AG_MAX_BLOB_SIZE), add `Limits::validate()` (reject zero / inconsistent values) and build the repository `Limits` from config in `Repository::assemble`. Make session.rs negotiate from `repo.limits()` instead of literals and replace the `5_000_000` in history.rs with a named field. Verify with a real repo test: init with a tight limits section, publish an over-limit blob/changeset against a real FsObjectStore/SQLite repo and assert rejection; assert `Negotiate` returns the configured values.

findings.excerpt: let ms = SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_millis() as i64).unwrap_or(0);
findings.problem: A wall clock before 1970 (broken RTC/VM) is silently turned into timestamp 0, and `as i64` silently truncates the u128 millis. `Timestamp::now()` is the production time source (ag-storage/src/clock.rs:19 SystemClock, ag-worker/src/attest.rs:64, ag-storage/src/object_store.rs:545 GC cutoff, ag-storage/src/s3/mod.rs:253), so lease expiry, GC grace windows and attestation timestamps would be computed from epoch 0 with no error: an error-swallowing fallback that fabricates a value.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the failure explicit: have `SystemClock` (the production caller that matters) detect `duration_since` errors and return a typed error / refuse to start (and have `ag doctor` check clock sanity), or at minimum use `i64::try_from` with saturation plus a logged error instead of `unwrap_or(0)`. Add a test with an injected time source proving a pre-epoch clock is reported, not zero.

findings.problem: The doc claims the reserved-component rule 'also holds on case-insensitive filesystems', but only ASCII case-folding is implemented (line 99 `eq_ignore_ascii_case`). On NTFS/Windows (a supported target per the Windows & portability work) `.git.` / `.git ` (trailing dot/space), the 8.3 alias `GIT~1` and `.git::$INDEX_ALLOCATION` resolve to the `.git` directory, and on macOS HFS+/APFS ignorable code points (e.g. U+200C inside `.g<ZWNJ>it`) and normalization-equivalent names do too. All of these pass `RepoPath::validate` (only control chars and backslash are rejected; MAX_PATH_LEN 4096 also exceeds Windows MAX_PATH 260; characters illegal on Windows such as `:<>|?*` and device names CON/NUL are accepted). Materializing such a path from an untrusted changeset re-opens exactly the code-execution vector the comment says is prevented. I found no other platform-alias handling anywhere in crates/ or docs/ (grep for ntfs/git~1/ignorable/NFC/casefold returned nothing relevant).
findings.proposed_fix: Either narrow the doc to what is true, or implement Git's verify_path semantics: reject components that, after stripping trailing `.`/space, ignorable Unicode code points and NFC/NFD normalization, equal `.git`/`.ag`; reject `git~N` 8.3 aliases and `:` (NTFS alternate streams); add a materialization-time check in the workdir writer for Windows reserved names/characters (or a platform-aware checkout validator). Verify on real Windows and macOS CI by attempting to check out a tree containing `.git.`, `GIT~1` and `.g<ZWNJ>it` and asserting no `.git` directory is created.

findings.problem: `principal()` builds the inner `Identity(..)` directly and bypasses `Identity::new` validation, so the documented invariant 'name is 1..=128 characters' is not upheld: `Identity::new("agent:#run1")` is valid ('#' is an allowed character and the name '#run1' is non-empty) but its principal is `Identity("agent:")` with an empty name. All agents named `agent:#x` collapse into one invalid principal `agent:`, and `principal()` is used in authorization comparisons (ag-server/src/api/agents.rs:21, jobs.rs:341, integration.rs:106, admin.rs:189; ag-agent/src/provenance.rs:92,131,193; ag-integrate/src/admin.rs:201,222). Not a mock, but a validation claim the code does not back.
findings.proposed_fix: Reject a name that starts with '#' in `Identity::new`, or make `principal()` go through `Identity::new(head)` and return a Result; add a unit test that `Identity::new("agent:#x")` is rejected and a proptest that `id.principal()` always satisfies `Identity::new(principal.as_str()).is_ok()`.

findings.problem: `kind()` re-parses the string and maps every unrecognised prefix to `IdentityKind::System` (the most trusted-sounding kind) instead of being total by construction; the accepted prefix list is duplicated in `new` (line 57: `["user", "agent", "service", "system"]`) and in `IdentityKind::prefix`, so the three can drift. The wildcard arm is unreachable today only because the field is private and `principal()` is the sole other constructor. A silent privileged fallback is the wrong failure mode for an authorization-relevant type. Borderline, hence low.
findings.proposed_fix: Store `IdentityKind` alongside the string in `Identity` (parse once in `new`), derive the accepted prefixes from `IdentityKind` (single source of truth), and make the impossible arm `unreachable!()` or remove it.

findings.problem: A deterministic-key constructor documented as 'for tests' is an unconditional public API of the production signing crate. Production code does not call it outside `KeyPair::load` (verified: other callers are ag-integrate/tests/policy.rs, ag-policy/src/eval_tests.rs and fuzz targets), but any downstream caller can mint a key from a guessable seed such as `[0; 32]` with no compiler or review barrier. The real component (`KeyPair::generate` / `load`) is available to tests, so the fixed-seed helper should not be reachable from release builds.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the public constructor private (used only by `load`) and expose a fixed-seed helper only behind `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "test-util"))]` (dev-dependencies of ag-policy/ag-integrate enable the feature). Alternatively use `KeyPair::generate()` in those tests and keep determinism only where vectors require it.

findings.excerpt:
/// A signing key pair. The secret is zeroized on drop.
...
secret: hex::encode(self.signing.to_bytes()),
...
let json = serde_json::to_vec_pretty(&file)...
...
serde_json::from_slice(&std::fs::read(path)?)...
let mut seed = [0u8; 32];
hex::decode_to_slice(&file.secret, &mut seed)...
findings.problem: Only the `SigningKey` field is zeroized (ed25519-dalek 3 with its default `zeroize` feature, verified in the vendored source). Every other copy of the secret is left in freed memory: the hex `String` in `KeyFile.secret` (lines 175-180, 210), the pretty JSON `Vec<u8>` in `save` (213), the `std::fs::read` buffer and the `KeyFile` String in `load` (239), and the local `seed` array passed by value to `from_seed` (243-245, 189). The doc sentence over-claims for a security crate.
findings.proposed_fix: Add the `zeroize` crate and wrap the transient secret material (`Zeroizing<String>`, `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>`, `Zeroizing<[u8;32]>`, `#[derive(ZeroizeOnDrop)]` on `KeyFile`), or reword the doc to 'the in-memory signing key is zeroized on drop; transient copies made while loading/saving are not'.

findings.problem: On non-Unix targets both the owner-only creation mode and the 'readable by others' check compile to nothing: a worker/agent private signing key (used by ag-worker/src/main.rs:171-172,308 and ag-agent/src/registry.rs:43-50) is written with inherited default ACLs and loaded without any permission check, silently. The workspace is explicitly being built and tested on Windows (task 'Windows & portability'), and the error text ('run `chmod 600`') is Unix-only. The doc says 'on Unix', so it is honest, but on Windows it is a silent no-op protecting a private key.
findings.proposed_fix: Implement the Windows equivalent: create the file with a security descriptor granting access only to the current user (CreateFileW with SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, or SetNamedSecurityInfoW with a protected DACL) and verify the DACL on load, returning `InsecurePermissions` otherwise; or, if the project chooses not to, fail loudly (or warn) on non-Unix and document the limitation in the user docs. Verify on the Windows CI runner with a test that inspects the ACL of the saved key file.

findings.problem: A test fixture ships in the production public API of `ag-changeset` (not cfg(test) and not feature-gated). Verified usage is test-only (ag-dag/src/tests.rs, ag-tree/src/tests.rs; the real implementation `StoreHistory<S: ObjectStore>` in ag-storage/src/history.rs is what the product uses), so nothing in the product path fakes history, but the type invites misuse by downstream code, and lock poisoning is turned into a panic via `.expect("lock")` (lines 56, 63). For ag-dag/ag-tree pure-algorithm unit tests an in-memory source is reasonable, but integration-level tests of history behaviour should use the real `StoreHistory` over FsObjectStore/SQLite, which are available to tests. Borderline, hence low.
findings.proposed_fix: Move `MemoryHistory` behind a `test-util` cargo feature (enabled via dev-dependencies of ag-dag/ag-tree) so it is not compiled into release artifacts; handle poisoned locks via `PoisonError::into_inner`; keep end-to-end history tests on the real `StoreHistory` + SQLite/Postgres harness in ag-storage/src/testing.rs.

findings.problem: The doc claims three backends: object store, 'metadata index' and in-memory fixture. The workspace contains implementations only for the object store (`StoreHistory` in crates/ag-storage/src/history.rs:31) and `MemoryHistory`; no `impl ChangesetSource` over the metadata index exists (grep over crates/ found none).
findings.proposed_fix: Either implement a `ChangesetSource` over the metadata store where it is needed (covered by a real SQLite/Postgres test) or remove 'the metadata index' from the doc comment.

findings.problem: Decoder caps are undocumented magic numbers that duplicate, but are not derived from, the real validation limits: `MAX_NAMESPACE_LEN = 128` repeats the literal in ag-types/src/identity.rs:152, and `MAX_AUTHOR_LEN = 160` is unrelated to Identity's actual maximum (128-char name plus the 'service:' prefix = 136). If either validation limit changes, decode and validation silently disagree. The `4096` preallocation cap on line 230 is likewise an unnamed constant. None of these caps appear in docs/architecture/object-format.md.
findings.proposed_fix: Export `Identity::MAX_LEN` / `Namespace::MAX_LEN` / `StreamName::MAX_LEN` from ag-types, derive `MAX_AUTHOR_LEN` from them, name the preallocation bound (e.g. `DECODE_PREALLOC_CAP`) and document the author/namespace caps in object-format.md; add a test asserting the longest valid Identity/Namespace round-trips through Changeset::decode.

findings.excerpt: description = "AgentGit: ag-types"
findings.problem: Package description is a name-echo placeholder; the same applies to crates/ag-object/Cargo.toml:3, crates/ag-changeset/Cargo.toml:3 and crates/ag-crypto/Cargo.toml:3 (other crates such as ag-sandbox, ag-server and ag-worker have real descriptions). This text is what cargo metadata, docs.rs and crates.io display.
findings.proposed_fix: Write real descriptions, e.g. ag-types: 'Validated identifiers, repository paths, identities and resource limits for AgentGit'; ag-object: 'Content addressing and strict canonical binary encoding'; ag-changeset: 'ChangesetV1 canonical encoding, decoding and validation'; ag-crypto: 'Domain-separated Ed25519 signatures and key files'.

findings.excerpt:
// Structurally invalid best-effort result: fall back to our tree.
        Err(_) => ours.clone(),
findings.problem: merge_full discards every error from Tree::from_entries. Only the file/directory case has a matching FileDirectory conflict pushed earlier. The other possible error, TreeError::TooManyEntries (merged result larger than limits.max_tree_entries), is swallowed with no conflict and no Err. Example: ours and theirs each add distinct files and are individually valid, but their union exceeds the limit. merge_trees then returns ours.clone() with an empty conflicts list, so is_clean() is true and every change from theirs is silently dropped. integrate.rs:406 computes head_tree.diff(&merged.tree), which is empty, so the 'clean merge' commits nothing from the proposal. This is silent data loss behind a swallowed error. The proptest strategies_agree uses Limits::default(), so it never exercises this branch.
findings.proposed_fix: Match the error instead of discarding it. For TreeError::TooManyEntries return Err (IoError wraps TreeError, since merge_trees already returns Result) or add a ConflictKind::TreeTooLarge conflict, so a clean result can never mean 'theirs was dropped'. Only FileDirectoryConflict may fall back to ours, and only when a FileDirectory conflict was reported for it. Verify with a real Tree/Limits test: Limits{max_tree_entries: N}, ours and theirs each add distinct files so the union is over N, then assert merge_trees returns an error or a non-clean result, never is_clean() with a tree equal to ours. Also add a Limits-parameterised case to the strategies_agree proptest.

findings.excerpt: let Ok(tree) = ours.apply(&ops, limits) else { return Ok(None) };
findings.problem: merge_incremental treats every Tree::apply failure as 'decline, run merge_full'. The intent is only to route file/directory collisions to the reference algorithm. TooManyEntries, and any other apply error such as a NoOpPut or DeleteMissing produced by an engine bug, is also swallowed and sent down the path that then hides it (see the finding on line 304). Real bugs and limit violations therefore turn into a silent fallback.
findings.proposed_fix: `match ours.apply(&ops, limits) { Ok(t) => t, Err(TreeError::FileDirectoryConflict{..}) => return Ok(None), Err(e) => return Err(e.into()) }`. Verify with the same limit-exceeding test as above, plus a debug assertion/test that no other TreeError variant occurs for ops that merge_incremental builds.

findings.excerpt:
//! Merge does not detect renames in this version; a rename is a delete plus an add, so a rename on one side and an edit on the other
//! conflicts.
findings.problem: The crate-level rustdoc says the opposite of the code. rename.rs implements rename detection, tree.rs plan_renames merges a moved-and-edited file at its new path, and ALGORITHM_VERSION is already 'ag-merge/2'. docs/architecture/merge-semantics.md and ADR-0005 describe the rename-aware behaviour. The semantics table at lib.rs:13-20 also omits the TooLarge, RenameRename and RenameDelete rows. The rustdoc on docs.rs and the module docs would mislead an auditor about what the 'pure, reproducible' algorithm does.
findings.proposed_fix: Rewrite the paragraph and table to match merge-semantics.md: rename-aware since ag-merge/2, exact and similar renames, the RenameRename and RenameDelete conflicts, no directory renames or copies. Better, include docs/architecture/merge-semantics.md via #![doc = include_str!(...)] or add a doc-sync test, so the two cannot drift again.

findings.excerpt: pub const ALGORITHM_VERSION: &str = "ag-merge/2+ag-diff/1";
findings.problem: The embedded diff version is a copy-pasted literal. ag-diff already exports ALGORITHM_VERSION = "ag-diff/1" (ag-diff/src/lib.rs:17), and ag-diff has no other user (grep: unused outside ag-diff). If ag-diff's behaviour is bumped to "ag-diff/2", every merge changeset will still record 'Merge-Algorithm: ag-merge/2+ag-diff/1', which is false audit metadata (integrate.rs:420, workspace.rs:276, virtual_ws.rs:221). The tunable constants that change results (MAX_TEXT_MERGE_SIZE, rename thresholds, MAX_EDIT_DISTANCE) are not reflected in the tag either.
findings.proposed_fix: Derive the string from ag_diff::ALGORITHM_VERSION at compile time (const_format::concatcp!, or a build-time macro). At minimum add a unit test: assert_eq!(ALGORITHM_VERSION, format!("ag-merge/{MERGE_REV}+{}", ag_diff::ALGORITHM_VERSION)). If merge parameters ever become configurable, fold a digest of the non-default values into the tag. Verify by bumping the diff const in a test build and checking that the test fails.

findings.excerpt: pub const MAX_TEXT_MERGE_SIZE: usize = 16 * 1024 * 1024;
findings.problem: A fixed 16 MiB per-side cutoff above which any both-sides-modified file is a TooLarge conflict. merge_trees receives &Limits, but ag_types::Limits has no merge fields, so an operator cannot tune it. Blobs up to max_blob_size (256 MiB by default) are accepted into the repo but cannot be merged beyond 16 MiB. The size check at tree.rs:501-505 also happens after all three blobs are read into memory (read_blob returns Vec<u8>), so the guard does not bound memory: up to 3 x 256 MiB is loaded first. The value is documented in merge-semantics.md and is determinism-relevant, which is why this is only low.
findings.proposed_fix: Add a versioned merge-parameters struct (for example MergeParams { max_text_merge_size, .. }, defaults equal to today's values) loaded from repository config and passed to merge_trees. Record any non-default values in the Merge-Algorithm trailer so the merge stays reproducible. Add a BlobIo::blob_size(&BlobId) (or length-limited read) so the size is checked before the bytes are loaded. Verify with a test using a real store: a 17 MiB file edited on both sides conflicts with the default and merges when the limit is raised.

findings.excerpt: pub const MAX_EDIT_DISTANCE: usize = 2048;
findings.problem: A fixed, non-tunable cap. Beyond it diff_hunks (lines 81-84) returns ONE hunk covering the whole trimmed middle. merge_text then sees both sides' giant hunks overlapping, so two edits that are far apart (for example 3000 changed lines in one place by each side) are reported as a content conflict although a clean line merge exists. Nothing tells the caller that the diff was not minimal. It is documented (module docs, merge-semantics.md), but the merge docs in ag-merge do not mention this false-conflict mode. The O(D^2) trace memory (trace: Vec<Vec<i32>>) is the reason for the cap.
findings.proposed_fix: Implement linear-space Myers (middle-snake divide and conquer) so the cap can be input-size based. If a budget is kept, make it a versioned parameter recorded in ALGORITHM_VERSION and return a 'not minimal' flag. Verify against the existing LCS oracle on inputs well above 2048 edits. Add a merge test where ours and theirs each rewrite 3000 lines at opposite ends of a 20k-line file and expect a clean merge.

findings.problem: Four rename-detection thresholds are compile-time constants with no config path, and the algorithm tag does not capture them. The 200-candidate cap means a refactor that moves more than 200 files at once (a normal monorepo package move) gets only exact-content renames. Moved-and-edited files then fall back to DeleteModify conflicts, which is exactly the situation rename-aware merge was added for. They are documented in ADR-0005 and merge-semantics.md and deliberately pinned for determinism, so this is borderline.
findings.proposed_fix: Move them into the same versioned MergeParams as the other merge limits (repo-level config with these defaults) and record non-default values in the Merge-Algorithm trailer. Consider replacing the hard candidate cap with a work-budgeted approach (size/exact-bucket prefilter) so large moves still match. Verify with a test that moves 500 slightly edited files on one side while the other side edits them, and expect a clean merge.

findings.excerpt:
TextMerge::Conflicted { regions, .. } => {
                return Ok(Resolution::Conflict(ConflictKind::Content { regions: regions.len() }));
findings.problem: The structured conflict data (ConflictRegion: base_line, base, ours, theirs; text.rs:21-22 'regions is the structured form') and the rendered markers are discarded; only the count survives. ConflictRegion is not used by any crate outside ag-merge (grep). ag-integrate::ConflictInfo is just {path, kind: String}, and workspace.rs:306 has to re-run merge_text to obtain the markers. The 'typed conflicts' therefore stop at the kind. An agent or API client sees 'content conflict (2 region(s))' but not where, so programmatic resolution (the product's agent-native pitch) lacks the data the engine already computed.
findings.proposed_fix: Carry the regions in Conflict (for example Conflict.regions: Vec<ConflictRegion>, or ConflictKind::Content { regions: Vec<ConflictRegion> }). Expose them through ConflictInfo, the HTTP/gRPC protocol and the SDKs, and stop the second merge_text in workspace sync. Verify end to end on a real server: ag preview / API returns the hunks, and an SDK test resolves a conflict from them.

findings.excerpt: let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(line);
findings.problem: unified_diff is built on lossy UTF-8 conversion. For text files in other encodings (Latin-1, Shift-JIS, mixed), whether text or binary is decided only by NUL bytes, so the diff shown by `ag diff` (ag-cli repo.rs:400-424) and the API (ag-integrate api_support.rs:95) contains U+FFFD replacement characters. The output is not byte-faithful: it cannot be applied with patch, and different byte sequences can render identically. A diff that silently rewrites content is misleading for a review product.
findings.proposed_fix: Return bytes (Vec<u8>) from a unified_diff_bytes variant for the CLI, which writes raw bytes. For JSON transports either classify invalid-UTF-8 files as 'Binary files differ' or return an explicit encoding or escaped form with a flag. Verify by diffing a real Latin-1 file and applying the CLI output with `git apply --check` / `patch` to reproduce the target bytes.

findings.problem: The 8192 is an inline magic number without a named constant. This heuristic decides Binary conflicts in merges (tree.rs:507), the rename-similarity eligibility (rename.rs:178) and diff display. It treats UTF-16 text as binary and a text file with its first NUL after 8 KiB as text. It is documented as a heuristic and mirrors git, so it is not presented as intelligence; this is borderline.
findings.proposed_fix: Introduce `pub const BINARY_SNIFF_LEN: usize = 8192;` documented as part of ag-diff/1. Optionally let repo attributes (a .agattributes-style mapping) override the classification. Verify with a test that includes a UTF-16 file and a file with a NUL at byte 9000.

findings.excerpt: out.extend_from_slice(b"<<<<<<< ours\n");
findings.problem: The conflict-marker side labels are literal 'ours' and 'theirs' (also line 120 for '>>>>>>> theirs'). render_conflict_markers takes no labels, so the real identity of each side (stream name, proposal id/title, merge base) that the engine knows is never shown. A person or agent resolving a marker file cannot tell whose change is whose. The base section is also never rendered although ConflictRegion.base exists. The workspace.rs:347 marker check is hard-wired to these literals.
findings.proposed_fix: Add labels (for example `render_conflict_markers(ours, theirs, labels: &MarkerLabels)`), filled by workspace sync with the stream and proposal names. Optionally support a diff3-style base section. Keep the detection prefix constants shared with workspace.rs. Verify with an `ag sync` end-to-end test on a real workspace that inspects the written marker file and `ag snapshot` refusal.

findings.excerpt: results.into_iter().filter(|id| flags[id] & STALE == 0 || flags[id] & RESULT != 0).collect();
findings.problem: The predicate is always true. Every id in `results` was pushed only after RESULT was set on it (lines 202-206), so `flags[id] & RESULT != 0` holds for all of them. The filter implies a staleness check that does not exist. Correctness is actually provided by the later pairwise is_ancestor pass, which is O(k^2 * walk). Dead logic like this hides which mechanism removes redundant bases.
findings.proposed_fix: Delete the filter and rely on (or document) the explicit redundancy elimination, or implement real stale-flag pruning and drop the quadratic pass. Verify with the existing merge_bases_match_naive proptest, extended with larger graphs (more than 14 nodes) and more criss-cross shapes.

findings.problem: Borderline. All ag-merge tests (and tests/scale.rs:15-27) run against an in-memory BlobIo. It is a faithful content-addressed store (hash_blob), not canned data, so it is a legitimate implementation. A real object store is feasible: ag-storage does not depend on ag-merge, and the production adapter RepoBlobs lives in ag-integrate. The merge unit and property tests therefore never touch the real read/write error paths (missing blob, failing write_blob) or a real store, other than what ag-integrate's tests happen to cover.
findings.proposed_fix: Keep Mem for the property tests (speed). Add an ag-merge integration test (dev-dependency on ag-storage's object store with a thin BlobIo adapter, on a tempdir) covering clean merge, content conflict, and rename+edit, plus a failing BlobIo that proves read/write errors surface as Err and are not swallowed.

findings.problem: The scale tests (this one and ag-tree/tests/scale.rs:25) are #[ignore]d, and ci.yml runs only `cargo test --workspace` (lines 40, 102), never `--ignored`. README.md:402 and ADR-0006 state measured performance ('measured at 100 000 files, an integration takes a few hundred milliseconds') that no CI job reproduces or guards. The correctness assertions inside (a clean merge at 500k entries, a rename plus an edit) never run either, so a regression in the incremental merge or rename path at scale would go unnoticed.
findings.proposed_fix: Add a CI job (release profile, scheduled or on core-crate changes) running `cargo test --release -p ag-tree -p ag-merge -p ag-integrate --test scale -- --ignored`, with explicit generous time-budget assertions (for example 100k-file merge under N ms), and keep a smaller 10k-entry variant in the normal test run. Alternatively soften the README wording to say the numbers are one-off measurements.

findings.excerpt: description = "AgentGit: ag-merge"
findings.problem: Placeholder crate metadata. The same template string is used in ag-tree/Cargo.toml:3 ('AgentGit: ag-tree'), ag-dag/Cargo.toml:3 ('AgentGit: ag-dag') and ag-diff/Cargo.toml:3 ('AgentGit: ag-diff'). The workspace sets no publish = false, so these would ship to a registry or docs.rs as meaningless descriptions.
findings.proposed_fix: Write real one-line descriptions, for example 'Deterministic three-way merge of text and trees with rename detection', 'Derived repository trees (flat sorted manifests) and tree ids', 'Changeset DAG algorithms: generation numbers, merge bases, ancestry', 'Deterministic Myers line diff and unified diff'. Add publish = false where the crates are not meant for a registry. Verify with `cargo package --list` / `cargo publish --dry-run`.

findings.excerpt:
// Notification-only topics have no in-process consumer.
                _ => Ok(()),
findings.problem: Every integration pushes a `stream.updated` outbox event (integrate.rs:555), and derive_pending then marks it dispatched (outbox_ack) although nothing delivers it. A grep of crates/ shows `outbox` is used only in ag-storage and ag-integrate: ag-server never reads the outbox and `outbox_history` has no caller outside tests. docs/architecture/storage.md:115 and adr-traceability.md:46 present the outbox as a transactional, at-least-once event source, but the only real consumer is tree derivation. The ack makes the event look delivered, so an external consumer could never receive it.
findings.proposed_fix: Either (a) build the real consumer: a dispatcher that delivers `stream.updated` / `changeset.published` to subscribers (webhook or SSE feed with a durable per-subscriber cursor, retry with backoff, and ack only after delivery), verified by a test that kills the subscriber mid-delivery against real PostgreSQL; or (b) stop writing events nobody reads and leave unknown topics pending instead of acking them. In either case correct storage.md:115 and adr-traceability.md:46 to say what is actually delivered.

findings.problem: docs/architecture/publication-and-integration.md:43 and storage.md:131 say derivation runs 'asynchronously (the outbox dispatcher)'. In fact there is no background dispatcher anywhere: derive_pending is called inline, in the request path, only after publish and integrate, with a hardcoded batch of 256. Its errors, and those of cache_tree, are discarded with `let _ =` and nothing is logged or counted. Failed events stay pending until some later publish or integrate happens to run another pass. The mutating caller blocks on this work and an operator sees no sign of failure.
findings.proposed_fix: Run a real dispatcher (a thread or task owned by ag-server, with an interval, backoff and a configurable batch size) and report failures through metrics and logs (outbox_pending, outbox_failed, last_error). Keep the inline call only as an optimisation that logs its error. Test it against real PostgreSQL by making derivation fail once and asserting the event is retried and the metric moves.

findings.excerpt: let _ = self.derive_pending(64);
findings.problem: Same inline best-effort derivation as integrate.rs:283. The batch of 64 is a magic number and the error is swallowed silently, so a failing derive pass after publication is invisible.
findings.proposed_fix: Use one named, configurable dispatcher batch size, and log or count the error. See the finding on integrate.rs:283.

findings.excerpt: let limits = Limits::default();
findings.problem: Repository::assemble, which is used by Repository::init and Repository::open and so by the CLI and server, always uses Limits::default() (blob 256 MiB, 100 000 ops, 16 parents, 64 KiB message, DAG depth 10 000 000, 10 000 changesets per publication, 2 000 000 tree entries). RepoConfig has no field for them and there is no env or flag override. An operator who needs larger blobs, or smaller ones to cap memory (S3 and the verifying store load whole objects), cannot change them. Because limits are part of validation, a different value would also change which histories are accepted.
findings.proposed_fix: Add an optional `limits` section to RepoConfig (additive, `format` stays 1, deny_unknown_fields, validated bounds) and pass it to Meta, FsObjectStore, S3Config and StoreHistory. Expose it via `ag init` / `ag config` and the server config, and document it in docs/architecture/object-format.md:87. Verify that a blob over a lowered max_blob_size is rejected on the real FS, S3 and PostgreSQL backends.

findings.excerpt: let mut opts = PgOptions { create_schema: create, ..PgOptions::default() };
findings.problem: ag-storage::PgOptions has connect_timeout (10 s), checkout_timeout (30 s), lock_timeout (30 s), statement_timeout (None), idle_in_transaction_timeout (600 s) and application_name ("agentgit"). MetaConfig::Postgres exposes only `pool_size`, so an operator cannot tune any of the others. lock_timeout and idle_in_transaction_timeout directly govern write-lock waits and how long a hung client holds the repository write lock in production.
findings.proposed_fix: Add optional fields to MetaConfig::Postgres (connect_timeout_ms, checkout_timeout_ms, lock_timeout_ms, statement_timeout_ms, idle_in_transaction_timeout_ms, application_name). Validate them (non-zero, upper bounds), apply them to PgOptions, and document them in docs/operations/postgres-and-s3.md. Cover them with a real-PostgreSQL test, for example a lock_timeout that yields MetaError::Retriable.

findings.excerpt: let mut cfg = S3Config::new(endpoint.clone(), region.clone(), bucket.clone(), credentials);
findings.problem: S3Config::new fixes max_retries (5), request_timeout (5 minutes) and list_page_size, and ObjectsConfig::S3 offers no way to change them. Operators of slow or throttled S3-compatible endpoints cannot tune retries or deadlines.
findings.proposed_fix: Add optional max_retries, request_timeout_ms and list_page_size to ObjectsConfig::S3, validate them, apply them to `cfg`, and document them. Test against a real S3-compatible server (MinIO) with an injected slow response.

findings.problem: The docs overstate what `ag verify` does. (1) The doc comment says 'the derived tree caches (recomputed from history)', but only the cached tree of each stream head is compared (lines 94-104). Keyframe trees and the trees of workspaces and pins are never checked. (2) docs/architecture/storage.md:123 says 'There are deliberately no foreign keys: referential consistency is checked by `ag verify`'. fsck checks nothing about pins, open proposals, workspace head/base, reviews, attestations, queue rows, intents or leases pointing at missing changesets. Only GC discovers a missing root, and then it aborts.
findings.proposed_fix: Implement the referential checks: every pin, open-proposal head and workspace head/base must exist in the object store and be a changeset; reviews and queue rows must reference an existing proposal; intents must reference existing objects; staged objects must exist. Verify every cached keyframe tree against a recomputation. Add tests that corrupt each reference with raw SQL (as tests/lifecycle.rs already does for streams) and assert a specific FsckIssue. Otherwise narrow the doc claims.

findings.problem: On non-Unix platforms scan always reports executable=false, and write_entry (lines 245-249) sets no mode there. Windows support is an in-progress goal (task #20). A repository checked out on Windows has its executable files reported as modified by workspace_status, because the scan says false and the head tree says true. A snapshot taken on Windows then silently strips the executable bit from files it did not touch. Symlinks on non-Unix at least fail loudly (line 239); the executable bit is lost silently.
findings.proposed_fix: On non-Unix, carry the executable flag over from the workspace head entry for unchanged content (the way git's core.fileMode=false does) by passing the previous Tree into scan. Add a way to set the bit explicitly, for example `ag chmod`. Verify on the real Windows CI runner with a checkout, scan and status round trip of an executable tree.

findings.excerpt: # Starts moto (a Python re-implementation of the S3 API, with conditional PUT,
findings.problem: All S3 coverage for ag-integrate (tests/common/mod.rs:85-104, tests/storage.rs, tests/lifecycle.rs: GC races, backup from S3) runs against moto, a Python simulator of S3. The CI `backends` job, ci.yml:102, uses it too. docs/architecture/adr-traceability.md:44 admits it is 'not against AWS or MinIO'. MinIO is a real S3-compatible server that is trivial to run in CI as a binary or service container. The behaviours the engine depends on are exactly the ones a simulator can get wrong: conditional PUT, CopyObject, LastModified resolution, and list pagination.
findings.proposed_fix: Add a CI job that runs the same suites with AG_TEST_S3_ENDPOINT pointing at a real MinIO (service container with a created bucket and user). Optionally run a nightly job against a real AWS S3 bucket using OIDC role assumption. Keep moto only as a signature cross-check. Update adr-traceability.md:44 and postgres-and-s3.md:209 once real servers are covered.

findings.excerpt: report.skipped.push(child_rel);
findings.problem: Sockets, FIFOs and device files are skipped and recorded in ScanReport.skipped, but every caller discards the report: workspace.rs:151 and :179 `let (now, _) = scan(...)`, and ag-cli/src/cmds/repo.rs:441. Nothing is surfaced to the user in `status`, `snapshot` or the API. The result is silent partial snapshots, and the same item is never reported twice.
findings.proposed_fix: Return skipped paths from workspace_status and snapshot (a field on Change or the snapshot result) and print them in the CLI and API responses. Test with a real FIFO created by mkfifo in a temporary directory.

findings.problem: `recover` loads at most 10 000 non-terminal intents, a magic number. Any intents beyond that are neither resumed nor expired, and the RecoveryReport does not say the list was truncated. After a large outage some operations are silently skipped.
findings.proposed_fix: Page through all non-terminal intents until none remain, or return a `truncated` flag in RecoveryReport. Name the constant. Test with more than the page size of stuck intents on real PostgreSQL.

findings.excerpt: const MAX_CAS_ATTEMPTS: usize = 8;
findings.problem: The retry budget for a compare-and-swap that keeps losing is fixed at 8 and cannot be tuned. Under many concurrent integrators the engine returns Error::Contention, and the tests need an outer retry loop of 50 (tests/engine.rs:390). No backoff or jitter is applied between attempts.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the attempt count configurable (repository or server setting) and add jittered backoff between retries. Cover it with a many-writer contention test on real PostgreSQL.

findings.excerpt: .unwrap_or_else(|_| Outcome::Invalid { reason: "unreadable result".into() }),
findings.problem: A stored intent result that fails to deserialize is silently turned into a plausible-looking `Invalid` outcome. The client is told its request was invalid, and a corrupt or incompatible record is hidden.
findings.proposed_fix: Return Error::Meta(MetaError::Corrupt(..)), or a dedicated Error variant, so corruption is surfaced and also reported by fsck. Test by corrupting an intents.result row.

findings.excerpt:
author: Identity::new("system:preview").expect("valid"),
                    timestamp: Timestamp::from_millis(0),
                    operation_id: "preview".into(),
findings.problem: merge_preview builds a throwaway merge changeset with a placeholder author, a timestamp of 0 and the operation id 'preview'. Its id is never persisted or returned (MergePreview carries only the tree), so this is harmless today. It is still placeholder data in a production code path, and it computes a changeset only to drop it.
findings.proposed_fix: Skip building the changeset when merge_meta is None, since only the tree and conflict data are needed. If a candidate id is ever exposed, derive it from the real intent metadata.

findings.excerpt: layout: Layout::new(std::env::temp_dir().join("ag-ephemeral")),
findings.problem: Repository::with_stores, which is public, gives the repository a fake on-disk layout: a fixed path under the system temp directory, shared by every process and every call. The doc comment says nothing is read from or written to disk. layout() and keys_dir() nevertheless return this phantom path, and Repository::backup is not guarded against it. backup.rs:92-95 takes the local-files branch when storage is None and would read from `<tmp>/ag-ephemeral/.ag/store/objects`, which is some other process's data if it exists.
findings.proposed_fix: Make `layout` an Option<Layout>, or add an explicit `detached` flag. Make layout(), reopen() and backup() return Error::Config('repository has no on-disk layout') for it. Remove the fixed temp path.

findings.excerpt:
pub fn ephemeral(namespace: Namespace, default_stream: StreamName, clock: Arc<dyn Clock>) -> Result<Self> {
        let objects: Arc<dyn ObjectStore> = Arc::new(MemoryObjectStore::with_clock(clock.clone()));
findings.problem: An in-memory repository (MemoryObjectStore plus in-memory SQLite) is a public API of the product crate, described as 'for tests and embedding'. Neither the CLI nor the server uses it. Its only caller is src/workdir/tests.rs, where a real `Repository::init` over a tempdir is just as easy (src/workdir/tests.rs:129 already does that).
findings.proposed_fix: Remove `ephemeral` from the shipped API, or gate it behind a `testing` cargo feature or #[cfg(test)], and use Repository::init with a tempdir in workdir/tests.rs.

findings.excerpt: pub struct Failpoints(Arc<Mutex<HashSet<String>>>);
findings.problem: Test fault-injection machinery is compiled into the production engine. There are seven `failpoints.hit(..)` sites: publish.rs:251, 340, 350, 372 and integrate.rs:254, 277, 281. There is also a public Repository::failpoints() accessor and an Error::Injected variant (error.rs:61). Each call takes a mutex on the hot path. Any embedding code with a Repository handle can arm a failure. The comment 'In production no failpoint is ever armed' is a convention, not an enforced guarantee.
findings.proposed_fix: Compile failpoints only under `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "failpoints"))]`, with zero-cost no-op stubs otherwise. Enable the feature from the crate's own tests via a dev-dependency on itself. Remove or gate Error::Injected.

findings.excerpt: fs::set_permissions(&tmp, fs::Permissions::from_mode(if entry.executable { 0o755 } else { 0o644 }))?;
findings.problem: Checked-out file modes are fixed at 0o755 or 0o644. They ignore the process umask and group or ACL conventions, so on shared hosts the result is more permissive than a normal create would be.
findings.proposed_fix: Derive the mode from the umask, as git does: 0o666 or 0o777 masked by ~umask. Or document the fixed modes in the workspace guide. Test with a restrictive umask on a real filesystem.

findings.excerpt:
idempotency_key: None,
                fencing_tokens: vec![],
findings.problem: run_queue always integrates with an empty fencing-token list, so a queued proposal that touches an exclusively leased path can never pass the lease check, whatever the caller holds. Such entries end up `blocked` forever, and there is no way to supply tokens through the queue API.
findings.proposed_fix: Store the tokens at enqueue time or accept them in `run_queue`, and pass them through to IntegrateRequest. Test with a leased path on real SQLite and PostgreSQL.

findings.excerpt:
if self.meta.kind() == MetaKind::Postgres {
            return Err(Error::Invalid(format!(
findings.problem: `ag backup` refuses repositories whose metadata is in PostgreSQL, which is the multi-replica production backend, and tells the user to run pg_dump. The refusal is honest and documented in postgres-and-s3.md:15. But docs/architecture/adr-traceability.md:52 marks 'Disaster recovery with consistent DB/object snapshots and reconciliation' as ✅ with `ag backup` as evidence, without saying that it does not work for PostgreSQL. Within ag-integrate, DR is implemented only for SQLite.
findings.proposed_fix: Implement the PostgreSQL path: a consistent dump (pg_dump in a REPEATABLE READ snapshot, or the COPY protocol inside one transaction) plus an object copy under the GC hold, and then restore plus `ag verify`. Verify it against a real PostgreSQL. Otherwise mark the traceability row 🟡 and state the limitation.

findings.problem: Un-named magic limit on the `~N` and `^N` revision suffix. The log walk is capped at `self.limits.max_dag_depth.min(5_000_000)` (line 184), a hidden second cap below the configurable limit.
findings.proposed_fix: Introduce named, documented constants, or derive both caps from Limits. Document them in the revision grammar help.

findings.problem: Fixed caps on the diff report (500 files, 4 MiB) and on history negotiation (MAX_NEGOTIATED = 1 000 000, line 22) cannot be tuned by an operator. The diff report does set `truncated`. blame.rs:35-37 likewise hardcodes MAX_BLAME_FILE_SIZE (4 MiB) and MAX_BLAME_LINES (100 000), exposed only as pub consts. Only max_commits is overridable. admin.rs:12 caps attestations per tree at 64 and admin.rs:115 caps proposal titles at 300 bytes.
findings.proposed_fix: Move these into one documented engine-limits structure, part of the repository and server configuration, with the current values as defaults. Expose them in the OpenAPI and CLI help, and test the truncation paths.

findings.excerpt:
let repo = Repository::with_stores(
        Namespace::new("acme/app").unwrap(),
        StreamName::new("main").unwrap(),
        meta,
        objects.store(),
findings.problem: The fixture behind most engine, policy, blame and lifecycle tests, `fx()`, uses ag_storage::testing::TestObjects. That is MemoryObjectStore unless an S3 endpoint is configured, and in-memory SQLite unless PostgreSQL is configured. The real filesystem store (FsObjectStore, the default product backend) is therefore exercised only by the few `disk_repo` tests, not by the bulk of the suite. A plain `cargo test` never runs the engine suites against the object store that ships by default.
findings.proposed_fix: Make TestObjects default to FsObjectStore in a tempdir, with ages driven by file mtimes (set via the filetime crate when the manual clock advances). Or run the suite in CI in a third matrix leg: PostgreSQL + FS.

findings.problem: Conflict.kind is documented as a stable, machine-readable enumeration, but every producer fills it with the human-readable Display text of ag_merge::ConflictKind (e.g. "content conflict (1 region(s))", "binary file changed on both sides"). See crates/ag-integrate/src/integrate.rs:402, workspace.rs:294 and virtual_ws.rs:200: `ConflictInfo { path: c.path.to_string(), kind: c.kind.to_string() }`, passed through unchanged by ag-server convert::conflict. The ConflictKind enum also has rename_rename and rename_delete variants that the proto does not list. Any SDK or client that switches on the documented values never matches.
findings.proposed_fix: Add a ConflictKind::code() returning the documented snake_case strings (content, both_added, delete_modify, binary, type_change, too_large, file_directory, rename_rename, rename_delete). Put that in ConflictInfo.kind and move the human text into a new `message` field. Add the two rename kinds to the proto comment. Verify with a real merge-conflict integration test per kind in ag-server/tests that asserts the wire value from the HTTP and gRPC responses, and regenerate the SDK schemas.

findings.problem: None of these topics are ever emitted. Events are a view of the audit log (crates/ag-server/src/api/events.rs:1-8, `topic: e.action.clone()`), so real topics are audit actions such as stream.integrate, proposal.create, lease.acquire, job.enqueue, run.start and policy.set. docs/protocol/agwp-v1.md lists the real ones, but this proto comment is the source for the generated SDK and OpenAPI docs. A client that follows it subscribes to topic filters that silently never fire.
findings.proposed_fix: Replace the example list with the real audit-action set. Better, generate it from a single exported constant list of audit actions and add a test that every action passed to audit_append appears in that list. Verify with an end-to-end test that subscribes with topics=["proposal.create"] and receives the event.

findings.excerpt:
// "running", "completed", "failed" or "stale" (abandoned: no heartbeat).
  string status = 7;
findings.problem: The protocol promises a "stale" run status, but the code writes "abandoned" (crates/ag-agent/src/registry.rs:202 `tx.run_finish(&run.run_id, "abandoned", Some("no heartbeat"))`, also asserted in ag-agent tests and ag-storage meta/agents.rs:38). The server passes the stored status through unchanged. Nothing in ag-server ever calls reap_stale_runs: its only caller is the manual CLI command `ag agent reap` (crates/ag-cli/src/cmds/agents.rs:144). Heartbeat-based staleness is therefore not enforced for remote agents, and the documented state is unreachable through the API.
findings.proposed_fix: Pick one status vocabulary and use it in the proto comment, the storage doc and the code. Add a background reaper task to ag-server with a configurable `agents.run_heartbeat_timeout` and interval, and have it call reap_stale_runs with a system actor. If you want an API to trigger it, expose that as an admin RPC. Verify with a server test that starts a run, stops heartbeating, and observes the status change and lease release over HTTP and gRPC.

findings.problem: SetPolicy is not naturally idempotent: ag-storage records.rs:367 policy_put always appends MAX(version)+1, and Policy docs state that a new policy version invalidates earlier attestations (policy.md). Retrying a SetPolicy after a lost response creates a second version and silently invalidates validations. Beyond that, about 19 mutating messages carry an `idempotency_key` that is "Accepted and ignored" (proto lines 170, 503, 524, 567, 603, 610, 696, 705, 712, 772, 809, 869, 883, 912, 952, 1014, 1087, 1187, 1315). Some are not safe to repeat: ModifyWorkspace makes a new changeset each time, ReviewProposal adds a review row, Enqueue adds a queue entry, SubmitProvenance adds a record, MintCredential mints a second credential, and RunQueue repeats the run. The fields look like a feature that does not exist.
findings.proposed_fix: Honor idempotency_key through the existing idempotent_create path (ag-server/src/api/mod.rs:41) for SetPolicy, ModifyWorkspace, ReviewProposal, Enqueue, SubmitProvenance, UpdateProposal and CompleteRun. Make SetPolicy a no-op when the canonical doc hash equals the current version. Remove the field from messages that truly cannot support it, or keep the field and document the retry hazard. Correct the Conventions paragraph. Verify with duplicate-request tests over HTTP and gRPC that assert one policy version, one changeset and one review.

findings.excerpt:
// e.g. missing_validation, approvals, missing_provenance, lease, not_allowed.
  string code = 1;
findings.problem: Blocker.code values are actually produced by ag-integrate types.rs `Blocker::from_unmet` from the serde tag of ag_policy::Unmet (eval.rs:60-62, snake_case): actor_not_allowed, author_not_allowed, failed_validation, missing_validation, insufficient_approvals, changes_requested, missing_provenance and too_many_changed_files, plus "lease". "approvals" and "not_allowed" do not exist, and the code set is not documented anywhere as a contract. The wire code is silently coupled to a Rust enum's serde representation, so renaming a variant breaks clients.
findings.proposed_fix: Add an explicit `Unmet::code()` with a fixed string per variant and use it in Blocker::from_unmet instead of the serde tag. List the complete set in the proto comment and docs/protocol. Verify with a test that enumerates every Unmet variant and compares its code to the documented list.

findings.excerpt:
const WALK_LIMIT: usize = 50_000;
...
Demo: ancestors(tx as &dyn Graph, &[h], WALK_LIMIT)
    .map_err(|e| ag_storage::meta::MetaError::Invalid(e.to_string()))?
findings.problem: predict() collects ALL ancestors of the stream head (lines 61-66), and ALL ancestors of every open proposal head (line 75), then diffs the sets. Because `ancestors` returns DagError::LimitExceeded past the limit, prediction fails with an Invalid error for any repository whose history exceeds 50,000 changesets. The limit is a fixed constant with no configuration. The algorithm is O(total history) per proposal even though only the changesets since the merge base matter.
findings.proposed_fix: Compute the exclusive ranges with a bounded walk. For each proposal use ag_dag::merge_bases(head, proposal.head), then walk_ancestors from each side and stop when reaching the base (or generation below the base), so the cost is proportional to the divergence. Make any remaining cap a documented config value and report truncation instead of failing. Verify with a real repo/test that has more than 50k changesets of shared history and a small divergence, and assert predict() succeeds quickly.

findings.excerpt:
let proposals: Vec<_> =
    tx.proposals_list(Some("open"), 1000)?.into_iter().filter(|p| p.stream == stream).collect();
findings.problem: The 1000 limit is applied BEFORE the per-stream filter and with no truncation signal. In a repository with more than 1000 open proposals across all streams, proposals are silently dropped, so overlaps are missed (false negatives) with no error or flag. The limit cannot be tuned.
findings.proposed_fix: Query proposals filtered by stream in SQL (or page through all of them) with no silent cap. If a cap is needed, make it configuration and return a `truncated` flag in Prediction/PredictResponse. Verify with a test that creates more than 1000 open proposals on other streams plus an overlapping pair on the target stream, and asserts the overlap is found.

findings.problem: Overlap paths are cut to 20 entries. The cut is documented in a doc comment (line 28) but the wire message (Overlap) has no `truncated` or total-count field, so clients cannot know that paths were dropped. It is a fixed, non-configurable magic number.
findings.proposed_fix: Add `total_paths`/`truncated` to Overlap in the proto and Rust struct, name the constant, and make it configurable or request-controlled (`max_paths` in PredictRequest).

findings.excerpt: let Ok(m) = PathMatcher::new(std::slice::from_ref(&l.scope)) else { continue };
findings.problem: lease_blockers is the integration gate for exclusive leases. If a stored lease scope fails to compile (for example after a globset upgrade changes accepted syntax, or a corrupt row), the lease is silently skipped, so the enforcement fails open. The same swallow is in predict.rs:115. Scopes are validated at acquire, but the gate should not depend on that.
findings.proposed_fix: Return MetaError::Corrupt (or treat the lease as matching every path, failing closed) when a stored scope does not compile, and log it. Verify with a test that inserts a lease row with an invalid glob directly and asserts that integration is blocked or errors.

findings.problem: Overlap of two globs is decided by comparing literal prefixes only. This is honest and conservative for advisory prediction, but acquire() (lines 76-78) also uses it for a HARD decision: refusing an exclusive lease. Disjoint globs with a common prefix, such as `src/**/*.md` and `src/**/*.rs`, are treated as overlapping, so legitimate exclusive leases are wrongly refused with a lease_conflict.
findings.proposed_fix: Implement a real glob-intersection emptiness check (compile both globs to regex/NFA via regex-automata and test intersection), and keep the prefix test only as a fast path that proves disjointness. Verify with property tests that compare against brute-force matching over generated path sets.

findings.excerpt:
/// Longest allowed lease duration.
pub const MAX_TTL_MS: i64 = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
findings.problem: The maximum lease TTL is a fixed 24 h with no operator configuration. acquire/extend also reject ttl_ms <= 0 (lines 68, 131) and the proto does not state a default or maximum for AcquireLeaseRequest.ttl_ms, so every client must pick a TTL blindly.
findings.proposed_fix: Move the maximum (and a default used when ttl_ms == 0) into server configuration, pass them into acquire/extend, and document both in the proto comment and the Negotiate limits.

findings.problem: The doc comment and the struct doc ("one <name>.json file each (mode 0600)") promise owner-only protection of agent private keys. It is applied only under #[cfg(unix)]; ag_crypto::KeyPair::save likewise sets mode 0600 only on Unix. On Windows, which the project builds and tests in CI, nothing restricts access and nothing warns.
findings.proposed_fix: On Windows, apply a DACL granting access only to the current user (SetNamedSecurityInfo/icacls equivalent or the `windows-acl` crate) to both the directory and the key files, and verify it on load as the Unix path does with `InsecurePermissions`. If that is not feasible, narrow the docs to say 'Unix only' and emit a warning on other platforms. Verify with a Windows CI test that reads the file's ACL.

findings.excerpt:
/// SHA-256 (hex) of the prompt; the prompt itself is not stored.
    pub prompt_digest: Option<String>,
findings.problem: The field is documented as a SHA-256 hex digest, but nothing validates it. attach() and attach_signed() accept any string, and the server's record_from_wire passes it through. ag-agent/Cargo.toml declares `hex` and `sha2` dependencies that are not used anywhere in the crate, which suggests the validation was intended and never written.
findings.proposed_fix: Validate prompt_digest as exactly 64 lowercase hex characters (reject otherwise with AgentError::Invalid) in both attach paths, optionally provide a helper that computes it from a prompt, and drop the unused `sha2`/`hex` dependencies if they stay unneeded. Verify with unit tests for valid and invalid digests.

findings.problem: The signing form is called canonical, but sorted keys come only from serde_json::Value's default BTreeMap. This silently depends on no crate in the build enabling serde_json's `preserve_order` feature (workspace Cargo.toml:62 enables a different feature, utoipa's `preserve_order`, which today does not affect serde_json). String escaping and number formatting are those of serde_json, not a specified canonicalization (such as RFC 8785), which remote Python/TypeScript/Go signers must reproduce byte for byte. docs/architecture/object-format.md:10 admits provenance is covered by Rust tests only, with no independent conformance vector, unlike attestations.
findings.proposed_fix: Implement an explicit canonical JSON writer (sorted keys, fixed escaping, integers only) or adopt RFC 8785 with a dependency, and add provenance vectors to tests/conformance/vectors.json that are generated by the Python reference and checked by Rust, TypeScript, Python and Go. Add a test that fails if key order stops being sorted.

findings.problem: The doc says compile failures are treated as 'nothing matches', but the code calls .expect("validated policy") seven times (lines 184-196), so an invalid policy panics inside the integration transaction. Policy fields are `pub` and Deserialize, so evaluate() can be called without validate(). Current callers use Policy::parse and are safe, but the contract in the doc is not what the code does.
findings.proposed_fix: Either change evaluate to return Result<Evaluation, PolicyError> (and have callers map it to a denial), or introduce a `ValidatedPolicy` newtype that can only be built by Policy::parse/validate and make evaluate take it, so the invalid case is unrepresentable. Update the doc to match.

findings.excerpt:
/// Target stream.
    pub stream: &'a str,
findings.problem: Facts.stream is filled in by callers (integrate.rs) and by every test, but evaluate() never reads it. It is a parameter that is accepted and ignored. Policy is already looked up per stream, so the field adds nothing and suggests stream-specific evaluation that does not happen.
findings.proposed_fix: Remove the field, or use it, for example in Unmet/Evaluation messages and in a check that the policy document is the one stored for that stream. Update callers and tests.

findings.excerpt:
/// Maximum accepted clock skew for attestation timestamps.
const MAX_FUTURE_SKEW_MS: i64 = 5 * 60 * 1000;
findings.problem: The tolerance for attestations dated in the future is a fixed 5 minutes. It is named and documented (policy.md says 'five minutes'), but an operator whose workers and server have different clock discipline cannot tune it per policy.
findings.proposed_fix: Add an optional `max_clock_skew_secs` to the Policy document (default 300, validated), pass it into passes(), and document it in policy.md. Borderline: the current value is documented behaviour.

findings.excerpt:
/// Maximum number of changed files for an autonomous change.
    pub max_files: u32,
findings.problem: With auto_integrate = true, a non-empty allowed_paths and max_files = 0 (the default), validate() accepts the document, but eval.rs:202 requires `max_files > 0` for within_autonomy, so agents can never integrate. The policy silently does nothing. 0 also means 'unlimited' for the sibling field max_changed_files, so the semantics are inconsistent and undocumented.
findings.proposed_fix: In Policy::validate reject auto_integrate (or any non-empty allowed_paths) with max_files == 0 and document that 0 means 'no autonomous changes'. Alternatively make max_files an Option and treat None as unlimited. Add a test in document.rs.

findings.problem: Two issues. The doc is inaccurate: ApprovalRules::default() sets min_for_agents: 1, so agent-authored changes also need one human approval (the guide policy.md says so, and the eval tests confirm it). More importantly, a stream with no stored policy gets this built-in allow-all default (ag-integrate integrate.rs:657, admin.rs:266), and ag-server has no deployment-level baseline policy option (config.rs has none), so an operator cannot make new streams secure by default.
findings.proposed_fix: Fix the doc comment. Add a server config key `policy.default_document` (validated with Policy::parse at startup) that is used wherever 'no policy stored' applies, and show it in `ag policy show` as version 0. Verify with a server test that starts with a restrictive baseline and sees an integration blocked on a fresh stream.

findings.excerpt:
/// Largest accepted object envelope (matches the engine's blob limit plus the envelope header).
    pub const MAX_OBJECT_BYTES: u64 = 256 * 1024 * 1024 + 64;
findings.problem: This is a hand-copied duplicate of ag_types::Limits::default().max_blob_size (256 MiB) plus an unexplained 64-byte header allowance. Nothing ties them together: ag-protocol does not depend on ag-types and no test compares them. The same is true of Negotiate in ag-server session.rs:44-45, which advertises `max_changeset_ops: 100_000` and `max_changesets_per_publication: 10_000` as literals copied from ag_types::Limits::default() instead of the engine's effective limits (the engine itself always uses Limits::default(), ag-integrate repo.rs:140, with no operator override). If either side changes, clients are told wrong limits. MAX_BATCH, MAX_PAGE_SIZE, DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE and CHUNK_BYTES are also fixed protocol constants that Negotiate advertises but operators cannot tune.
findings.proposed_fix: Build the Negotiate Limits from the engine's real ag_types::Limits (exposed by Repository/App) and from config, so that advertised equals enforced. Derive the envelope allowance from ag_object's header size constant. Add a test asserting advertised == enforced for every field, and expose the page/batch caps in ag-server config.

findings.problem: The fallback for statuses from non-AGWP peers (a proxy, load balancer or gateway) is a partial mapping: AlreadyExists, FailedPrecondition, Aborted, OutOfRange, DataLoss and Unimplemented all become `internal`, and ResourceExhausted always becomes rate_limited (never quota_exceeded). That makes retryable() wrong for Aborted/Unavailable-like cases and misreports permanent errors. The doc says 'best effort', so it is a known gap, not a bug in the intended contract.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the mapping total over tonic::Code (the inverse of grpc_code, choosing the primary AGWP code per gRPC code). Add a table-driven test over all 17 tonic codes.

findings.excerpt:
const JSON_FIELDS: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
    ("agwp.v1.Event.payload_json", "payload"),
    ...
const BYTES_FIELDS: &[&str] = &["agwp.v1.ObjectChunk.data", "agwp.v1.FileChange.content"];
findings.problem: The lists of fields that get JSON/base64 handling are maintained by hand and do not come from the descriptor. A new `*_json` or `bytes` field added to the proto and forgotten here silently becomes a raw string or an array of numbers in the HTTP/JSON mapping, and no check detects it. Today all five `_json` fields and both `bytes` fields are covered.
findings.proposed_fix: In build.rs, iterate the compiled FileDescriptorSet and derive the lists (fields whose name ends in `_json` and all `bytes` fields), or fail the build if a field matching those rules is absent from the lists. Verify by temporarily adding an unlisted field.

findings.problem: Several request fields have server-side defaults and caps that the protocol never states and the operator cannot configure. ClaimJobRequest.lease_ms: 0 becomes 120 s and is capped at 1 h, and wait_ms is capped at 30 s (ag-server api/jobs.rs:35-37). HeartbeatJobRequest.lease_ms has the same default and cap. ReadHeadRequest.wait_ms is capped at 30 s (api/streams.rs:14). DiffRequest.context (line 457): 0 is treated as 3 and the maximum is 100 (api/tree.rs:149), so zero context lines cannot be requested. SubscribeRequest.heartbeat_ms is silently clamped to at least 1000 (api/events.rs:95). MintCredentialRequest.ttl_secs: 0 becomes min(max, 1 h for agents, 24 h otherwise) (api/admin.rs:218).
findings.proposed_fix: Document each default and cap in the proto comments and in the Negotiate limits, move them into ag-server configuration, and make DiffRequest.context `optional uint32` so 0 is expressible. Verify against the server with tests that read the advertised values.

findings.problem: client_name and client_version are accepted and then ignored: ag-server session.rs negotiate() never reads them (not logged, counted, or put in metrics). Only supported_versions and features are used. The fields give the appearance of client tracking that does not exist.
findings.proposed_fix: Record them in request logs/trace attributes and a low-cardinality metric (client_name only), or remove the fields. Verify by checking the log/metric in an ag-server observability test.

findings.excerpt: if Authorizer::roles(p, std::slice::from_ref(b), &b.repo.replace('*', "x")).contains(&b.role) {
findings.problem: Cross-reference to the Principal.roles contract (proto line 104, 'Effective roles per repository pattern'). Whoami decides whether a role binding applies to the caller by substituting every '*' in the repo pattern with the letter 'x' and asking the authorizer about that made-up repository name. This is a heuristic that depends on the pattern semantics; it does not evaluate the binding directly. It is in ag-server, flagged because it implements a protocol field.
findings.proposed_fix: Add an Authorizer method that evaluates a binding's subject match against the principal directly (without a sample repo) and returns the applicable (pattern, role) pairs. Verify with tests for exact, prefix and '*' patterns, and for group roles.

findings.excerpt: //! The S3 object store against a real S3-compatible server (`scripts/s3-test.sh`   [scripts/s3-test.sh:7: "# Starts moto (a Python re-implementation of the S3 API, with conditional PUT,"]
findings.problem: The only 'real server' S3 suite (tests/s3.rs, CI job 'backends') talks to moto, a Python mock/re-implementation of AWS S3, not to an actual S3 implementation. The header of the test file calls it 'a real S3-compatible server'. Conditional PUT (If-None-Match), CopyObject-onto-itself with REPLACE, LastModified resolution/refresh, ListObjectsV2 paging, SigV4 verification and the GC race are exactly the behaviours where mocks and real servers differ, and the GC-safety argument of the whole S3 backend rests on the CopyObject age refresh. A real S3-compatible server (MinIO single static binary, Garage, SeaweedFS, Ceph RGW in a container) is trivially available in CI (the PostgreSQL side already uses a real postgres cluster).
findings.proposed_fix: Add MinIO (pinned release binary or container, started by scripts/s3-test.sh next to or instead of moto, with signature verification on and versioning/object-lock variants) and run tests/s3.rs, tests/object_lock-style GC race tests and the workspace suite against it in the 'backends' CI job with AG_REQUIRE_BACKENDS=1. Keep moto only as an extra, clearly labelled mock. Fix the wording of tests/s3.rs:1 and scripts/s3-test.sh:7 to say what is actually used. Verify by running `AG_TEST_S3_ENDPOINT=<minio> cargo test -p ag-storage --test s3` and the GC race test `s3_gc_cannot_delete_an_object_a_writer_just_reput` green.

findings.excerpt:
//! An S3-compatible [`ObjectStore`] (Amazon S3, MinIO, Ceph RGW, Cloudflare R2,
//! …) over a blocking HTTP client, with hand-rolled AWS Signature V4.   [docs/operations/postgres-and-s3.md:209-211: "Verified against **PostgreSQL 16** and **moto** ... Not yet run against Amazon S3, MinIO or other PostgreSQL versions"]
findings.problem: Code docs, ADR-0004, the operations guide intro and the README present Amazon S3, MinIO, Ceph RGW and Cloudflare R2 as supported backends, but the only server the code has ever been run against is moto; the ops doc itself admits it was 'not yet run against Amazon S3, MinIO'. Support is claimed for four products that were never exercised, and the PostgreSQL claim is limited to one major version.
findings.proposed_fix: Either add real-server CI jobs (MinIO; PostgreSQL 14/15/16/17 matrix via pg-test.sh; optionally a scheduled job against a real Amazon S3 bucket / R2 using repository secrets) and keep the claim, or narrow the claim in s3/mod.rs:1, docs/operations/postgres-and-s3.md:5 and ADR-0004 to what is verified, with a compatibility matrix generated from the CI jobs.

findings.excerpt:
//! The S3 client against a scripted local HTTP server: wire format, signing,
//! retries, and refusing to treat failures as success. No real S3 needed.
findings.problem: A hand-written in-process HTTP 'Fake' (struct Fake at line 52) answers canned bodies. For fault injection (503, dropped sockets, 200-with-<Error> from CopyObject) a scripted peer is justified, because a real server cannot be told to fail on demand. But the same fake is also used to assert happy-path protocol facts (key layout, If-None-Match, ListObjectsV2 pagination and 'LastModified' handling, delete_if_older_than reading Last-Modified, the 501 fallback, addressing styles). These tests encode the author's belief about S3's wire behaviour and would pass even if real S3 behaved differently.
findings.proposed_fix: Keep the scripted server strictly for fault-injection/retry cases and say so in the header. Move the protocol-fact assertions (layout, listing, paging, LastModified-based age, conditional create fallback) to tests/s3.rs so they run against a real MinIO (see the moto finding); only keep fast unit checks that need no server.

findings.problem: Staging files in <root>/tmp are never reclaimed: nothing in the workspace deletes them (only backup.rs recreates the empty dir). A crash/kill between File::create and rename leaves an orphan (up to blob-limit 256 MiB, mode 0444 once set_permissions ran), and every error return after creation (set_permissions, rename, sync_dir) also leaks the tmp file because there is no cleanup guard. The documented invariant 'empty when idle' is therefore false after any crash, and disk usage grows without bound.
findings.proposed_fix: Wrap the tmp file in a guard that removes it on every error path, and add FsObjectStore::reap_tmp(older_than) that takes gc.lock exclusively (writers hold it shared for the whole put, so under the exclusive lock every tmp file is by definition orphaned) and deletes everything in tmp/; call it from FsObjectStore::open and from `ag gc`. Verify with a test that kills a writer mid-put (failpoint/subprocess) and asserts tmp/ is empty after reap, plus the existing fs_leaves_no_temp_files test.

findings.excerpt:
.unwrap_or_else(|| Timestamp::from_millis(0));   // list()
...
.unwrap_or(0);   // delete_if_older_than(), line 404
findings.problem: When the file system cannot report an mtime (modified() error, or a time before the epoch) the store invents the Unix epoch. list() then reports a fabricated 'modified = 1970' and delete_if_older_than() treats the object as infinitely old (0 < cutoff), so garbage collection will delete an unreachable object without honouring the grace period that protects objects a writer just re-put. A missing fact is turned into the most dangerous value instead of an error.
findings.proposed_fix: Return StoreError::Io (or a dedicated error) when modified() is unavailable, in list() make ObjectInfo.modified fallible or skip the object from GC candidates, and in delete_if_older_than refuse to delete (return Ok(false) with a logged reason) if the age cannot be determined. Test with a store on a file system/fake metadata that lacks mtime.

findings.problem: On non-Unix targets (Windows is an in-progress target) the directory fsync after rename is a silent no-op and the 0444 hardening is skipped, yet durability() returns the same static contract everywhere: name 'local-fsync', survives 'kernel panic' and 'power loss (fsync honoured by the disk)', and docs/architecture/storage.md:25 documents 'rename -> fsync of the directory' unconditionally. On Windows a rename is not durably persisted by this code, so the advertised guarantee is not backed. Additionally set_modified on a handle opened read-only (File::open) is not guaranteed to work on Windows (needs FILE_WRITE_ATTRIBUTES), which would break the idempotent re-put path; unverified.
findings.proposed_fix: Implement the Windows equivalent (open the directory with FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS and FlushFileBuffers, or MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH) or make durability() report a weaker contract on cfg(not(unix)) (survives: process crash only). Open the file with write access for set_modified. Verify on the Windows CI job (task: Windows & portability) with the existing put/reput tests.

findings.problem: StoreError::Injected is documented as a test-harness fault, but no harness ever creates it; its single construction site is the production FsObjectStore::put reporting a genuine failure of the system RNG. Operators would read 'injected fault' for a real entropy failure, and the variant name hides the real cause.
findings.proposed_fix: Map the RNG failure to StoreError::Io(std::io::Error::other(..)) or add a StoreError::Entropy variant with an accurate message; delete the Injected variant (or move it behind a test-only feature if a failpoint really needs it).

findings.excerpt:
impl Default for PgOptions {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            pool_size: 8,
            connect_timeout: Duration::from_secs(10),
            checkout_timeout: Duration::from_secs(30),
            lock_timeout: Duration::from_secs(30),
            statement_timeout: None,
            idle_in_transaction_timeout: Duration::from_secs(600),
            application_name: "agentgit".into(),
            create_schema: true,   // wiring: ag-integrate/src/storage.rs:231-234 sets only create_schema and pool_size
findings.problem: PgOptions exposes seven operational knobs, but the only configuration path (storage.meta in .ag/config.json -> ag-integrate open_meta) sets pool_size and create_schema and nothing else. connect_timeout, checkout_timeout, lock_timeout (write-lock wait), statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_timeout and application_name are fixed at the library defaults, so an operator cannot tune lock wait, statement limits or idle-in-tx for a busy or slow database, although docs/operations/postgres-and-s3.md describes these defaults as things 'you may want to know about'. The reference table lists only pool_size.
findings.proposed_fix: Add the fields to MetaConfig::Postgres (connect_timeout_ms, checkout_timeout_ms, lock_timeout_ms, statement_timeout_ms, idle_in_transaction_timeout_ms, application_name) with the current values as documented defaults, validate in StorageConfig::validate, pass them to PgOptions in open_meta, and extend the reference table. Verify with an integration test against the real PostgreSQL (tests/storage.rs) that a configured 500 ms lock_timeout yields MetaError::Retriable.

findings.problem: The SQLite busy timeout is a literal 30 s in init_sqlite with no parameter on Meta::open/open_with and no config key; the PostgreSQL counterpart is at least a PgOptions field. Operators of many-process SQLite setups (the default backend) cannot lengthen or shorten the wait before MetaError::Retriable, and the 128-statement cache size is an undocumented magic number.
findings.proposed_fix: Introduce a SqliteOptions { busy_timeout, statement_cache } (defaults 30 s / 128 as named constants), add Meta::open_with_options, thread it from storage.meta (kind sqlite) config in ag-integrate and from ag-server's config, and document the keys. Test with two real handles on one file: one holds BEGIN IMMEDIATE, the other must return Retriable after the configured timeout.

findings.excerpt:
max_retries: 5,
request_timeout: Duration::from_secs(300),
list_page_size: 1000,   // http.rs:129 `.timeout_connect(Some(Duration::from_secs(10)))`; http.rs:305-309 backoff: `50u64.saturating_mul(1 << attempt.min(6)).min(3000)`
findings.problem: S3Config has max_retries, request_timeout and list_page_size, but ag-integrate's open_s3 (storage.rs:300-306) sets only prefix, limits, path_style and ca_bundle, so these three are fixed defaults for every deployment and absent from the documented storage.objects reference. The connect timeout (10 s) and the retry backoff schedule (50 ms base, 3 s cap, 50% jitter) are hard-coded inside the client and cannot be changed even from Rust.
findings.proposed_fix: Add connect_timeout, backoff_base/backoff_max to S3Config (named, documented constants as defaults) and expose max_retries, request_timeout, connect_timeout and list_page_size as storage.objects keys in ag-integrate (ObjectsConfig::S3), validating ranges; update the reference table. Verify against MinIO with a throttled/slow proxy or tc that a short request_timeout surfaces StoreError::Remote.

findings.problem: The result of pg_advisory_unlock(_shared) is discarded. The lock lives on one long-lived dedicated session that is reused afterwards; if the unlock statement fails while the connection stays alive (statement_timeout/query_canceled, a role-level statement_timeout, server-side error), the session lock is never released and every other process's collector/writers block indefinitely until this process exits, while the in-memory state says it was released.
findings.proposed_fix: On unlock error mark the pooled session broken (drop it) so the server releases all its advisory locks; log the error. Add a test in tests/object_lock.rs that makes the unlock statement fail (e.g. SET statement_timeout on the session via a helper, or terminate between lock and unlock) and asserts another connection can then take the lock.

findings.problem: The object-lock connection ignores all connection settings an operator would configure for the metadata connection (connect/checkout timeouts, statement timeout, idle-in-transaction) and hard-codes the search_path schema 'public' and application_name 'agentgit-object-lock' in connect(). It cannot be tuned independently and a locked-down role without access to 'public' still works only by accident.
findings.proposed_fix: Accept &PgOptions in PostgresAdvisoryLock::connect_with and pass the same configured options (see PgOptions wiring finding); use the repository schema for search_path instead of the literal 'public'.

findings.excerpt: .keepalives_idle(std::time::Duration::from_secs(60));   // and pg/mod.rs:298 `if self.stmts.len() >= 512 { self.stmts.clear(); }`
findings.problem: TCP keepalive idle time (60 s) and the per-connection prepared-statement cache cap (512, which also drops the whole cache at once) are unnamed literals that are not part of PgOptions, so they cannot be adapted to firewalls/NAT idle timeouts or to statement cardinality.
